reports.main_answer_reason: The report gives a substantial, predominantly source-supported reconstruction of the opposing ownership and possession claims, the original grant's documentary uncertainty, the 1861 agreement, equal-share revenue and possession entries, Mehrab's testimony, the 1893 Chief Court litigation, and the later trial and High Court findings. It correctly preserves the distinction between prior adjudications and the withheld target disposition, and identifies the adverse-possession submission as unresolved in the permitted view. Its principal confirmed substantive defect is the placement of the 1877 paragraph 5 joint-tenure and revenue arrangement under the 1861 agreement, which materially distorts the settlement chronology. It also omits important evidence supporting the competing title theories, especially the affirmative 1877 joint-ownership history, the specific 1903–08 partition restriction, earlier adverse-possession and Bhandadar pleadings, the basis of the 1893 decree, and the unchallenged sale testimony. The description of a statutory partition right and the precise identification of the target appellate institution are not independently established by the allowed view, but neither is sufficient here to make the entire substantive answer wrong. The appropriate assessment is therefore PARTIAL, without inferring any withheld final result.
uncertainties: The permitted record reports a September 11, 1861 agreement in the plaintiffs' pleading but separately identifies an earliest documentary agreement dated September 28, 1861. Their precise relationship cannot be settled from the supplied excerpts alone.
The original 1822 grant was unwritten, and no contemporaneous record of its terms is supplied. The exact proprietary interests initially conferred cannot be conclusively established.
The earlier Divisional Judge's affirmance is reported, but the text of that judgment is expressly absent from the record.

The permitted view does not include the target appellate court's treatment of the High Court's ownership findings, the partition restriction, the binding force of the 1893 judgment, or the adverse-possession submission.

The available procedural heading does not expressly identify the target institution as the Supreme Court. This nominal detail cannot be independently verified using only the permitted source excerpts.

The evidence contains both early sole-owner descriptions and subsequent joint-proprietorship records. The report and permitted record do not justify converting either category into an unqualified final appellate finding.

serious_errors.materiality: Joint possession is documented, but the exact record year is not explicit in the permitted excerpt. Its chronological force could matter; severe distortion is unresolved.

important_omissions: The report does not discuss paragraph 2 of the earlier Wajib-ul-arz, which expressly contemplated partition by co-sharers according to Khewat shares (S238d7f39e142). This is a material qualification to any broad characterization of the original settlement arrangement as prohibiting co-sharer partition.

The report omits that the 1861 agreement was verified by Dalmir, Dilmor, Alif Khan and Phusa, who were described as proprietors (Sa3f85bc956f4). These early documentary descriptions matter when comparing the plaintiffs' exclusive-ownership theory with the defendants' coownership claim.

The report does not address the P. 4 Jama apportionment statement, which initially described Dalmir as sole owner but also stated that other named cultivators became entitled to profits and liable for losses (S5b8cecc74c8e). This complicates a simple division between Dalmir's revenue rights and the other branches' produce rights.

The report does not explain the full 1890–1893 procedural sequence: Alif Khan and Sharif Khan's rejected partition applications, Alif Khan's ensuing one-fifth-share suit, the subordinate and divisional court decisions, and the Chief Court's amended declaration recognizing Alif Khan's one-fifth share subject to the existing Wajib-ul-arz restrictions (S39b2e2b00a49, Se8038316b346, S644c4367bcb6). This limits its assessment of the earlier adjudication's scope.

The report omits that the 1893 Chief Court decree was made on defendants' admission during arguments and that the court distinguished general division by co-sharers from separation of shares among Dalmir's sons (S644c4367bcb6, Sc2d688a625ac). These details matter when evaluating what the earlier judgment actually decided and any CPC Section 11 argument.

The report omits the Dalmir-side pleadings in the earlier litigation alleging adverse possession and characterizing the other parties as Bhandadars or village servants (Se8038316b346). Those were historical allegations, but their existence is important in reconstructing the development of competing possession and title theories.

The report reports Mehrab's acquiescence without identifying the documented transaction: Mehar Singh, a Sharif Khan descendant, sold his half share to Chhote Khan and Bhola, who were Mehrab's co-plaintiffs (S7c5282f5f79b). The seller-purchaser relationship is relevant to the significance of nonchallenge.

The report states the High Court reversal but omits the precise four-fifths proprietary share recognized for the contesting defendants and the dismissal of the suit (S4b2b3a6e0136, S1e2ef59ee816). These are material aspects of the prior appellate disposition.

The report does not substantially assess the evidentiary tension between the asserted acquisition of the defendants' shares by adverse possession and the historical records of joint possession, acknowledged proprietary entries and earlier one-fifth-share adjudication. The allowed evidence supports identifying that tension but does not establish the ultimate adverse-possession result.

The report does not note that the later Wajib-ul-arz was admittedly signed by the parties' ancestors (S2395fb536e92). This historical assent evidence matters to the competing arguments over the original restrictions, although it does not independently establish consent to their 1938–39 renewal.
reports.main_answer_reason: Historical arguments and prior findings are reported; major ownership-decree and adverse-possession analysis gaps remain. No withheld target disposition is invented.
uncertainties: The original 1822 grant's precise proprietary terms cannot be reconstructed from a grant instrument because the permitted record expressly states that no writing or contemporaneous evidence exists.

The sources refer to an agreement dated September II, 1861 in the plaintiffs' pleaded account (Sfce6b2ed4bf5) and an agreement dated September 28, 1861 in the detailed documentary account (S417aaf0285ac). The latter supports the report's date, but the difference and exact documentary identity should not be silently resolved.

The exact relationship between the 1861 tenure description, its partition provisions, the 1877 Wajib-ul-arz and the more explicit 1903–08 restriction is not fully settled by the report's compressed treatment. Historical restrictions must be evaluated by their particular content and period.
The effect of the 1938–39 renewal is reported as a High Court finding of nonbinding effect because of nonagreement. The withheld target court's treatment cannot be inferred.

The 1893 Chief Court judgment recognized a one-fifth share subject to specific temporary restrictions. Whether its actual determinations satisfy every applicable preclusion requirement in the later litigation cannot be conclusively decided from the report's discussion alone.

The allowed material records the assertion of more than 56 years of adverse possession but does not supply sufficient findings establishing the necessary character, exclusivity and continuity of possession or the resulting title.

Mehrab's admitted nonobjection does not by itself establish intentional inducement, reliance or the parties against whom statutory estoppel could operate. The report's expressly tentative legal suggestion remains unproven.

The supplied case excerpts identify no agricultural lease dispute. The absence of a ruling on agricultural-lease provisions does not establish that such provisions were relevant or applicable to the historical proceedings.
No conclusion is drawn about the withheld target court's reasoning, final ownership determination, partition entitlement or appellate disposition.

reports.main_answer_reason: The report provides a substantially source-grounded reconstruction of the competing title claims, the four-settlement documentary sequence, joint-possession entries, testimony, earlier Chief Court proceedings, trial decree, High Court reversal and unresolved target-court disposition. It generally preserves the distinction between a party's contention and an attributed judicial finding. Its important limitations are the material misstatement of the 1903–08 partition entitlement as an intra-Dalmir division, the invented Panchayat consent requirement, temporal displacement of later settlement evidence, and insufficient examination of the adverse-possession contention against the documented ownership and possession evidence. It also omits the earlier decree's basis in admissions and the historical Bhandadar/adverse-possession pleading. These problems prevent a fully supported substantive assessment, but the report does not purport to establish the withheld final outcome and much of its central procedural and evidentiary account remains correct.
uncertainties: The target court's reasoning, disposition and assessment of the competing title theories are withheld; no ultimate ownership or partition outcome is inferred.
The exact terms and full proprietary implications of the unwritten 1822 grant are unavailable.
The report's reference to papers being lost 'During the first Settlement (1839-42)' may be temporal or merely a transition into discussion of those records.
The placement of paragraph 5 in the 1863 discussion creates ambiguity even though its substantive content is supported in the later settlement materials.
The report's phrase 'binding precedent' may be shorthand for binding effect inter partes or may improperly claim broader precedential authority.
The complete lower-court adjudication of the appellants' 56-year adverse-possession contention is not established by the supplied excerpts.
Whether the report intended Alif Khan to stand for Amir Khan's entire branch or to identify a separate founding branch is uncertain, despite the inaccurate founder list.
The permitted excerpts do not expressly identify the receiving appellate forum by name, despite identifying Civil Appeal No. 61 of 1951.
The exact legal reach of earlier decisions to all present descendants and claims cannot be settled from the summarized procedural extracts alone.
No inference is made that supplied but uninvoked statutory provisions necessarily apply to the historical dispute.

reports.main_answer_reason: The report provides a substantially source-grounded reconstruction of the competing title claims, the four-settlement documentary sequence, joint-possession entries, testimony, earlier Chief Court proceedings, trial decree, High Court reversal and unresolved target-court disposition. It generally preserves the distinction between a party's contention and an attributed judicial finding. Its important limitations are the material misstatement of the 1903–08 partition entitlement as an intra-Dalmir division, the invented Panchayat consent requirement, temporal displacement of later settlement evidence, and insufficient examination of the adverse-possession contention against the documented ownership and possession evidence. It also omits the earlier decree's basis in admissions and the historical Bhandadar/adverse-possession pleading. These problems prevent a fully supported substantive assessment, but the report does not purport to establish the withheld final outcome and much of its central procedural and evidentiary account remains correct.
uncertainties: The target court's reasoning, disposition and assessment of the competing title theories are withheld; no ultimate ownership or partition outcome is inferred.
The exact terms and full proprietary implications of the unwritten 1822 grant are unavailable.
The report's reference to papers being lost 'During the first Settlement (1839-42)' may be temporal or merely a transition into discussion of those records.
The placement of paragraph 5 in the 1863 discussion creates ambiguity even though its substantive content is supported in the later settlement materials.
The report's phrase 'binding precedent' may be shorthand for binding effect inter partes or may improperly claim broader precedential authority.
The complete lower-court adjudication of the appellants' 56-year adverse-possession contention is not established by the supplied excerpts.
Whether the report intended Alif Khan to stand for Amir Khan's entire branch or to identify a separate founding branch is uncertain, despite the inaccurate founder list.
The permitted excerpts do not expressly identify the receiving appellate forum by name, despite identifying Civil Appeal No. 61 of 1951.
The exact legal reach of earlier decisions to all present descendants and claims cannot be settled from the summarized procedural extracts alone.
No inference is made that supplied but uninvoked statutory provisions necessarily apply to the historical dispute.
